lesson.title: The Attitudes We Don't Know We Have
lesson.summary: Implicit attitudes are automatic, often unconscious evaluations of people or groups that can diverge from a person's consciously stated beliefs, most commonly studied using the Implicit Association Test, though how well that test predicts any individual's actual behavior has become a genuine point of scientific debate.
lesson.body:
Explicit attitudes are the beliefs and evaluations we would report if you asked us directly, "I believe everyone deserves equal treatment regardless of background." Implicit attitudes are different: automatic associations, often outside full conscious awareness or conscious control, that can shape quick judgments and reactions even when they clash with what a person consciously believes and would sincerely endorse. Building on the previous two chapters, a person can consciously and sincerely reject the stereotypes and prejudice discussed earlier while still carrying implicit associations shaped by years of cultural exposure, media portrayals, and everyday socialization. This is not necessarily hypocrisy. It reflects how associative memory works, quietly absorbing patterns from the surrounding environment in ways that are not fully under a person's deliberate control.

The most widely used tool for measuring implicit attitudes is the Implicit Association Test, or IAT, developed by Anthony Greenwald, Debbie McGhee, and Jordan Schwartz and introduced in 1998. The test measures how quickly people can pair concepts together, for instance pairing images of faces from different racial groups with positive or negative words, on the logic that people respond faster when pairing concepts that are already closely linked in memory and more slowly when pairing concepts that clash with existing associations. The IAT became enormously influential both as a research tool and as a public education tool, popularized in part through the Project Implicit website, where millions of people have taken versions of the test.

Here the honest scientific picture matters more than the popular one. The IAT's ability to predict any individual person's actual discriminatory behavior has been the subject of real and substantial debate among researchers. Meta-analyses examining this question, including a widely cited one led by Frederick Oswald and colleagues in 2013, found that IAT scores are, on average, only weakly correlated with individual discriminatory behavior, considerably weaker than the test's public reputation might suggest. Even some of the researchers who helped develop the IAT have acknowledged that it is not well suited to diagnosing or predicting a given individual's likely behavior, while suggesting it may still be more informative when looking at patterns across large groups than when used as a precise instrument on any one person.

None of this means the underlying concept of implicit attitudes is invalid. The broader idea, that people carry automatic associations which can diverge from their consciously stated beliefs and can leak into split second judgments and reactions, has fairly broad support and matters for understanding subtle, unintentional forms of bias. What deserves real caution is treating the IAT specifically as a precise, settled measurement of any one person's inner prejudice, since the evidence does not support that level of individual precision. That same caution about the limits of automatic, unexamined mental processes carries directly into the final concept in this unit, the just-world phenomenon, where a different kind of automatic belief shapes how people judge others without much conscious deliberation at all.
